newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans get Black Forest foretaste of euro money.
newsitem.headline: Germans get Black Forest foretaste of euro money.

text.p: Anyone curious to know what life may be like if Europe's planned single currency becomes reality should forget the corridors of power in Bonn, Brussels or Paris and head for this idyllic Black Forest town.

Under a two-week long scheme which began on Tuesday, the 20,000 citizens of Waldkirch and anyone who cares to visit can shop with specially issued euro coins although their deutsche marks are still legal tender as well.
Around 50 businesses in the town have agreed to take part in the scheme, organised by the local savings bank, and are displaying prices in euros as well as marks.

In a cobble-stoned lane off the main street, one bakery with a European flag fluttering proudly outside was even advertising special offers for euro-spending shoppers. "Eight pretzels for four euros!" a poster proclaimed.

If European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) moves forward as planned, citizens in participating countries would face a similar situation between January and July 2002 as their national currency is phased out and the real euro is phased in.
In Waldkirch, demand for the two special coins -- issued in denominations of three and 25 euros and exchanged at a rate of two marks to one euro -- was immense.
By lunchtime, the savings bank had sold out of its stock.
"It's got people talking and that was our aim all along," mayor Richard Leiblinger said.

He acknowledged some Germans, especially the elderly, felt uneasy about giving up a currency which has brought rock-hard stability after the nightmare of pre-war hyperinflation and said he hoped the scheme would put some minds at rest.
Few Waldkirch citizens seemed willing to part with their euros, preferring to keep them as collectors' items or gifts.
Reporters from the Bonn press corps, who invaded the sleepy settlement en masse, searched in vain for a shopper carrying out a genuine transaction in euros.
The closest they came was a woman buying some rolls but her purchase had been set up by a desperate television camera team.

While shoppers may have been reluctant to dish out their euro cash, local officials said they would be more than happy to accept it. "Parking illegally will cost you 30 marks -- or 15 euros," declared traffic policeman Armin Allgaier.
"I think it's more of interest to collectors," electrical store sales clerk Maria Burger said. "I can't see the people here buying them at the bank and then just spending them again."
Waldkirch took its cue from its French twin town Selestat in the Alsace region which carried out a similar scheme in May.
The scheme has been timed to mark the 30th anniversary of Waldkirch's twinning with Selestat.

The 25 euro coin is 40 mm in diameter, 10 mm wider than the three euro coin which has a silver centre surrounded by a golden rim. Both coins sport the coats of arms of Selestat and Waldkirch on one side and Waldkirch's castle on the other.

"A real discussion can only be provoked by tangible things. The issues themselves are very abstract, so schemes like this one are very helpful," said Dietrich Elcherlepp, the local member of the European parliament.
In the local Waldkircher Anzeiger weekly newspaper, the project was buried in the second section alongside results from local bowling clubs and a report on autumn fashion trends.
Some residents had reservations about monetary union itself.
"It may make sense but looking at things from an emotional point of view, I prefer my deutsche mark," said Helmut Disch, the co-owner of a hotel perched in woodland above the town.
